'''''Atocion armeria''''', commonly known as '''Sweet William catchfly''', is a species of [[plant]] in the family [[Caryophyllaceae]]. Originally a native of Europe, it has become widespread in the United States. A small-growing [[form (botany)|form]] is known as a '''dwarf catchfly'''. The name comes from the way in which small insects are trapped by the sticky sap exuded onto the stem. Although it has been identified as a [[carnivorous plant]] in the past, it is not currently regarded as such.<ref name="Williams">Williams, Amy. (1913). [https://kb.osu.edu/dspace/bitstream/1811/1779/1/V13N05_097.pdf Carnivorous plants of Ohio]. ''The Ohio Naturalist'', 13(5): 97-99.</ref>

==Description==
[[File:Silene_armeria_Sturm21.jpg|thumb|left|Figure from book ''Deutschlands Flora in Abbildungen'']]
[[File:Siléne_arméria.JPG|thumb|left|Bracteate [[inflorescence]]]]
[[File:Lietuvos_gamtai_reversas.jpg|thumb|right|The Lithuanian former 50 [[litas]] [[silver]] [[coin]] featuring Sweet William catchfly<ref>[https://www.lb.lt/en/coins/coin-dedicated-to-the-sweet-william-catchfly 9999.lt / Coin dedicated to the Sweet William Catchfly] Retrieved 5 February 2026.</ref>]]

The plant is between {{convert|20 and 70|cm|abbr=off|frac=2}} in height. [[Leaves]] are numerous, ranging from {{convert|2.5–5|cm|abbr=on|frac=4}} long, elliptic, oval, or narrowly oval, smooth. The blooming period in [[British Isles]] is from June to October. Clusters of pink or lavender flowers arranged somewhat openly or compactly at the end of stems. [[Plant stem|Stem]] hairless (glabrous) or slightly hairy with sticky areas, especially just below the cluster.

==Distribution and habitat==
A plant [[Indigenous (ecology)|native]] of Europe in roadsides, weedy places. Has been introduced to North America and later [[Escaped plant|escaped cultivation]] to become an [[invasive species]].

Perennial in [[United States Department of Agriculture|USDA]] plant [[hardiness zone]]s 5 to 8.
